methods.label: Count by the parity of the product
methods.explanation:
A sum is even exactly when its two terms have the same parity. Thus \(ab+c\) is even when \(ab\) and \(c\) are both odd or both even.

There are three odd choices, \(1,3,5\), and two even choices, \(2,4\). Because the selections are made with replacement, the \(5^3=125\) ordered triples \((a,b,c)\) are equally likely.

The product \(ab\) is odd exactly when both factors are odd. This gives \(3\cdot3=9\) ordered pairs \((a,b)\). Each can be followed by any of the three odd choices for \(c\), producing \(9\cdot3=27\) favorable triples.

Of the \(25\) ordered pairs \((a,b)\), the remaining \(25-9=16\) have even product. Each can be followed by either even choice for \(c\), producing \(16\cdot2=32\) more favorable triples.

These two cases are disjoint and cover every way the sum can be even. Therefore the probability is
\[
\frac{27+32}{125}=\boxed{\frac{59}{125}},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
